subject: geography
promptStrong: Give me an exam-style {board} {level} {subject} question on {lo}, then mark my answer against the mark scheme.
promptWeak: Explain {lo} for {board} {level} {subject} simply, with a clear example and the most common mistake students make.

questions.q: In the disaster-risk (risk = hazard x vulnerability / capacity) equation, risk is reduced by:
questions.explain: Because capacity to cope is the denominator, raising it lowers overall disaster risk.

questions.q: Resilience to tectonic hazards is best described as the ability of a community to:
options: Predict the exact time of every earthquake
Absorb, adapt to and recover from a hazard event
questions.explain: Resilience is the capacity to withstand, adapt to and bounce back from a hazard impact.

questions.q: Why are 'rare earth' and critical minerals increasingly strategically important?
options: They are essential for renewable technologies and electronics but concentrated in few countries
They are only used in jewellery
questions.explain: Critical minerals underpin batteries, magnets and electronics, yet their concentrated supply creates geopolitical vulnerability.

questions.q: At a constructive (divergent) oceanic plate margin, the characteristic landform and process is:
options: Deep ocean trench and explosive volcanism
Mid-ocean ridge with effusive basaltic eruptions
questions.explain: Diverging plates allow basaltic magma to rise, creating mid-ocean ridges with gentle effusive eruptions.

questions.q: What does 'energy transition' typically refer to today?
options: Moving power stations to new locations
The shift from fossil fuels towards low-carbon and renewable sources
Switching homes from gas to oil
questions.explain: The contemporary energy transition is the structural move away from fossil fuels towards renewable and low-carbon energy.

questions.q: Which seismic wave type is the fastest and is the first to be recorded at a seismograph?
questions.explain: P-waves are compressional and travel fastest, so they arrive first at a seismometer.

questions.q: Which describes the concept of 'energy security' most fully?
options: Uninterrupted availability of affordable energy with diverse and reliable supply
questions.explain: Energy security means consistent access to affordable energy, supported by diversity and reliability of sources and supply routes.

questions.q: At a collision (continental-continental) margin such as the Himalayas, there is generally:
options: Crustal thickening and fold mountains with no subduction
questions.explain: Two continental plates of similar density collide, buckling and thickening the crust into fold mountains without significant subduction.

questions.q: How does climate change threaten water security?
options: It has no effect on water
It alters precipitation patterns, shrinks glaciers and increases droughts and floods
questions.explain: Warming shifts rainfall, melts the glaciers that feed rivers, and intensifies both droughts and floods, stressing water supplies.

questions.q: Tsunamis are most commonly generated by:
options: Vertical displacement of the sea floor during a submarine earthquake
questions.explain: Sudden vertical movement of the sea floor, typically at subduction zones, displaces the water column and generates a tsunami.

questions.q: Why is food security about more than just total production?
options: It also requires availability, access, utilisation and stability of supply
questions.explain: Food security needs adequate availability, physical and economic access, proper nutrition and stable supply over time.

questions.q: What is an 'energy pathway'?
options: The career of an energy engineer
A walking route to a power station
The route by which energy travels from producer to consumer
questions.explain: An energy pathway is the flow of an energy resource, such as a gas pipeline or oil tanker route, from source to market.

questions.q: Conservative (transform) margins produce earthquakes but no volcanoes because:
options: Plates slide past one another, so no crust is created or destroyed
Magma is too viscous to erupt
Plates move apart, allowing magma up
questions.explain: At conservative margins plates move laterally past each other; crust is neither created nor subducted, so there is friction-driven seismicity but no magma generation.

questions.q: What is 'virtual water'?
options: The hidden water embedded in the production of goods and food
questions.explain: Virtual water is the volume used to produce a commodity, so importing goods effectively imports water used elsewhere.

questions.q: How can desalination improve water security, and what is its drawback?
options: It produces freshwater from seawater but is energy-intensive and costly
questions.explain: Desalination converts seawater to freshwater, boosting supply, but it consumes large amounts of energy and money.

questions.q: The key distinction between earthquake magnitude and intensity is that magnitude measures:
options: The depth of the focus only
The energy released at the source, while intensity measures felt/observed effects
The felt and observed effects at the surface
questions.explain: Magnitude (e.g. moment magnitude) quantifies energy released at the source, whereas intensity (e.g. Mercalli) describes the shaking felt and damage observed.

questions.q: Which margin type is associated with the deepest-focus earthquakes and explosive andesitic volcanoes?
questions.explain: Subduction at an oceanic-continental destructive margin produces a Benioff zone of deep earthquakes and explosive andesitic stratovolcanoes.

questions.q: What is the 'circular economy'?
options: A system that designs out waste by reusing, recycling and remanufacturing resources
Trade that only flows in one direction
An economy based only on circular coins
questions.explain: The circular economy keeps materials in use through reuse, repair and recycling, contrasting with the linear take-make-dispose model.

questions.q: What does 'peak oil' refer to?
options: The point at which global oil production reaches its maximum before declining
The highest oil price ever recorded
questions.explain: Peak oil is the hypothesised point of maximum global production, after which output is expected to fall.

questions.q: Which force, generated by the sinking of a dense, cold oceanic plate at a subduction zone, is now regarded as the dominant driver of plate motion?
questions.explain: Slab pull arises as a cold, dense subducting slab sinks into the mantle and is considered the most significant force moving plates.

questions.q: The point within the Earth where an earthquake originates is the:
questions.explain: The focus (hypocentre) is the underground point of rupture; the epicentre is the point on the surface directly above it.

questions.q: What is a major sustainability concern with intensive industrial agriculture?
options: Soil degradation, water pollution from fertilisers, and high energy use
questions.explain: High-input farming can degrade soils, pollute water through nutrient run-off and depend heavily on fossil-fuel-based inputs.

questions.q: Why might unconventional gas extraction such as fracking be controversial?
options: It raises concerns over water contamination, induced seismicity and methane leakage
questions.explain: Fracking is contested due to risks of groundwater pollution, small earthquakes and fugitive greenhouse-gas emissions.

questions.q: The water-food-energy nexus describes:
options: The interdependence whereby managing one resource affects the others
A trade agreement between three nations
questions.explain: The nexus highlights that water, food and energy systems are interconnected, so a decision in one affects supply in the others.

questions.q: Liquefaction during an earthquake occurs when:
options: Saturated, loose sediment temporarily behaves as a fluid under shaking
questions.explain: Ground shaking raises pore-water pressure in saturated unconsolidated sediment so it loses strength and behaves like a liquid.

questions.q: Multiple-hazard zones (e.g. the Philippines) experience compounded risk because they:
options: Lie far from any plate boundary
Are exposed to several physical hazards plus high vulnerability
questions.explain: Such regions face overlapping tectonic and climatic hazards combined with social and economic vulnerability.

questions.q: What is the main aim of 'resource stewardship'?
options: Managing resources sustainably to balance present needs with future availability
questions.explain: Resource stewardship promotes sustainable management so resources remain available for future generations.

questions.q: Ridge push (gravitational sliding) operates because newly formed oceanic lithosphere at a mid-ocean ridge is:
options: Denser and colder than older lithosphere
Elevated and slides down the sloping asthenosphere away from the ridge
questions.explain: At ridges the hot, raised lithosphere slides down the flanks under gravity, pushing the plate away from the ridge axis.

questions.q: The Pressure and Release (PAR) model explains a disaster as the intersection of a natural hazard and:
options: A process that releases vulnerability rooted in social, economic and political conditions
questions.explain: PAR traces vulnerability from root causes through dynamic pressures to unsafe conditions, which meet the hazard to create disaster.

questions.q: What distinguishes physical water scarcity from economic water scarcity?
options: Economic scarcity means too little water; physical means high prices
Physical scarcity means too little water; economic scarcity means lack of investment to access available water
questions.explain: Physical scarcity is an absolute shortage of water, whereas economic scarcity is failure to access water that exists due to inadequate infrastructure or investment.
